Open a GPX track, pick a date and start time, and Ridge Light estimates when you walk in direct sun or terrain shade, then shows the result on OsmAnd\'s map.

Walking times follow the rule behind hiking-sign times (DIN 33466): 4 km/h on the flat, 300 m up or 500 m down an hour, whichever takes longer plus half the other.
The slider sets any pace in between. Times include your breaks.
A break stays at its place on the route when you change the start time or pace, and the light during it counts in the totals.
To add one at a place, drag along the profile and tap “Break here”.
The break stays at this place when you change the start time or pace.
Ridge Light then combines the terrain with the cloud forecast: sun under a clear sky stays sun, under broken cloud it becomes “sun and clouds”, and overcast or fog hides it.
For this, the coordinates of up to six points of your route are sent to Open-Meteo (open-meteo.com), for every route you open while Clouds is on. Nothing else is sent.

The number is sun; after “+”, sun between clouds. ★ most sun, with sun between clouds counted half.
Days more than a week ahead are greyed: their forecast is rough.
When are you in the sun on your hike, and when do the mountains hide it?

Terrain: for each point of the route, at the time you get there, Ridge Light looks from your eyes towards the sun across elevation data up to 45 km away, allowing for the curve of the earth, and checks whether a ridge is in the way.
Timing: your start time and the rule behind hiking-sign times (DIN 33466: 4 km/h on the flat, 300 m up or 500 m down an hour), scaled by your pace. Breaks stay at their place on the route.

Clouds (when switched on): the forecast cloud cover at different heights for a few points of the route, at your altitude and time. Terrain sun under a clear or thin sky stays sun; under broken cloud it becomes “sun and clouds”, counted half when comparing start times and days; overcast or fog hides it.
Trees, buildings and snow are not modelled. The elevation data is a few tens of metres coarse, so narrow gorges and single rocks can be missed.
Cloud forecasts are coarse too: models work on a grid of a few kilometres and on levels a few hundred metres apart, often misplace low fog, and get rough more than a week ahead.
No account, no tracking. Terrain tiles for the area of your route are downloaded from Amazon\'s open-data server, which therefore sees that area; they are kept on the phone.
Only while Clouds is on, the coordinates of up to six points of your route are sent to Open-Meteo for the forecast. Nothing else is sent.
Results go to OsmAnd through its app interface, on the phone.
Terrain Tiles: Mapzen/Tilezen on AWS Open Data (SRTM, GMTED, ETOPO1, NED and others)
